title: Analysis of Anthropic's Text Watermarking in Claude: Technical and Ethical Concerns
summary: The article critically examines Anthropic's implementation of semantic watermarking in its Claude AI models to comply with EU regulations. The watermarking technique alters word choices during text generation, subtly favoring certain words over others based on a secret-key system, which can later be probabilistically detected. The author argues that this approach compromises the quality, precision, and integrity of AI-generated text, as it prioritizes watermarking over optimal word selection. The article also critiques the EU regulation driving this change, highlighting its impracticality and potential to harm honest users while failing to deter malicious actors.
key_points: Anthropic's watermarking technique uses steganography to alter word choices during text generation, embedding detectable patterns without relying on invisible Unicode characters.
The system divides potential word choices into 'green' and 'red' lists, slightly favoring 'green' words to create a probabilistic watermark detectable only with a secret key.
The watermarking affects all text generated by Claude longer than 200 tokens (~150 words), including private conversations, potentially degrading text quality and precision.
The author argues that no two synonyms are semantically identical, and watermarking forces suboptimal word choices, undermining the craft of writing.

The EU's 'Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content' is criticized as impractical, as it may harm honest users while being easily circumvented by dishonest actors using non-compliant tools.

Google's SynthID, a similar watermarking system for text, is also scrutinized for its claims of imperceptibility, with the author contending that subtle word changes are noticeable and degrade text quality.
The article highlights tools like Declaude, which can remove watermarks, demonstrating the futility of such regulations in preventing misuse while burdening legitimate users.
